name: Duckface theory

card.summary: The idea that the duckface pose sharpens the jaw, hollows the cheeks and implies a projected maxilla, making a face look more defined in photos.
card.note: A community theory about photo posing; no published study tests the claimed effect.

quick.overview:
Duckface is the pouted-lip, sucked-in-cheek pose common in selfies. On looksmax.org, some members argue it is popular because it creates the look of a more developed mid and lower face.

The claimed mechanics are three: jutting the jaw forward for a tighter jawline, sucking in the cheeks so the cheekbones show, and pushing the upper lip out to suggest a projected upper jaw.
quick.how: People adopt the expression in photos or while walking around, sometimes alongside chosen angles, lighting and filters. Some members also ask how to get the same look without the pose, naming lower body fat and masseter growth as routes.
quick.risks: The pose itself is harmless; the discussion concerns appearance. Some members note that it can look unnatural to viewers. No studies test whether it alters facial structure or how attractive a face is rated.

lead: Duckface is a pose in which the lips are pushed out and the cheeks are usually sucked in, common in social-media profile pictures from the 2010s.[1] Encyclopedic coverage describes it as typically intended to look alluring, though it can also be ironic or a way to hide self-consciousness.[1]

Duckface theory is the looksmaxxing reading of that pose. A looksmax.org member argued that people use it because it creates an impression of strong mid-facial and lower-third development, by jutting the jaw out, hollowing the cheeks and pushing the top lip forward to imply maxilla projection.[2] Another member wrote that doing it while walking around tightened the skin and made his jaw look squarer.[3]
No published study has tested these claims. The theory is a community explanation for a photo trend.

chain: Jut the jaw and pout the lips
Cheeks pulled in, jaw and lip pushed forward
Face reads as more angular in the image
angle.text: Members say the pose borrows the visual cues of a prominent jaw, high cheekbones and projected upper jaw. In a photo it can change how the lower face reads, similar to angle and lighting choices.

infobox: Sharper jaw, visible cheekbones, projected maxilla

paras: The pose has precedents: fashion models have long used exaggerated pouts, and the 1994 film Four Weddings and a Funeral nicknamed a character Duckface, while Zoolander (2001) parodied model pouts.[1] The New York Times covered the selfie trend in 2011, and OxfordDictionaries.com added the term in 2014.[1]

The looksmax.org thread listing the three mechanics says the pose gives the illusion of a forward face and defined cheekbones, and adds that filters, angles and lighting serve the same end.[2] Replies in other threads ask how to get that look without the expression and suggest lower body fat and masseter growth, with surgeries such as buccal fat removal or genioplasty also raised.[3]
One poster comments that the expression can make the mouth look odd; the thread's author calls the whole practice a way to exploit how much weight society places on looks.[2]
No studies found. Research on the topic is limited to the use of the term duck face for a lip-protrusion display in capuchin monkeys, reported in encyclopedic coverage.[1]

timeline.event: Four Weddings and a Funeral nicknames a character Duckface.[1]
The New York Times publishes Duck Hunting on the Internet.[1]

lore.intro: The idea appears in looksmax.org threads that treat the pose as an unconscious jawline and cheekbone enhancer.[2][3]

claims.claim: Duckface creates the illusion of a better mid and lower face
claims.believers: A member says the pose juts the jaw, hollows the cheeks and pushes the lip out to imply maxilla projection.[2]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined whether the pose changes perceived facial structure.

claims.claim: Doing duckface tightens the skin and squares the jaw
claims.believers: A member says wearing the expression while walking made his jaw look squarer.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this.
